parts:
Hi Marc,

Thank you so much for your reply. I got this part, but I have run into some few more questions and I would be really grateful if you can provide your opinion on this. I will start will a brief summary of what I am doing. 

I am using pcountOpen to estimate 1) temporal trends in abundance and 2) effects of areas under different land cover land use and weather factors on temporal variation in abundance of sage grouse. These birds were surveyed along 108 fixed transects once per year for 11 years. Now I have different models. 

Now to find most parsimonious model, I did 
         aictab(list of candidate models) and I got 2 models with deltaAIC <4.

Actual code:
aictab(m1.full)

Model selection based on AICc
                                                          Delta_AICc
m1.crop.grass.year.ppt.minTemp.date     0.00
m1.grass.year.minTemp.maxTemp.date   2.18

Now I am doing model averaging using modavg
Actual code:
cand.mod<-list(m1.crop.grass.ppt.minTemp.date, m1.grass.minTemp.maxTemp.date)
modnames<-c("m1","m2")
avg.mod.Intercept<-modavg(parm.type="lambda",cand.set = cand.mod,modnames = modnames,parm="Int")
avg.mod.crop<-modavg(parm.type="lambda",cand.set = cand.mod,modnames = modnames,parm="crop")
avg.mod.grass<-modavg(parm.type="lambda",cand.set = cand.mod,modnames = modnames,parm="grass")
avg.mod.gamma.year<-modavg(parm.type="gamma",cand.set = cand.mod,modnames = modnames,parm="year_survey")
avg.mod.gamma.pp<-modavg(parm.type="gamma",cand.set = cand.mod,modnames = modnames,parm="ppt_survey")
avg.mod.gamma.min<-modavg(parm.type="gamma",cand.set = cand.mod,modnames = modnames,parm="minTemp_survey")
avg.mod.gamma.max<-modavg(parm.type="gamma",cand.set = cand.mod,modnames = modnames,parm="maxTemp_survey")
avg.mod.p.date<-modavg(parm.type="p",cand.set = cand.mod,modnames = modnames,parm="dates_survey")
avg.mod.p.Int<-modavg(parm.type="p",cand.set = cand.mod,modnames = modnames,parm="Int")
The same result can also be obtained using model.avg
Actual code:
avg<-model.avg( m1.crop.grass.year.ppt.minTemp.date,m1.grass.year.minTemp.maxTemp.date)

1) My first question is regarding interpretation of the result. So I am getting 
lambda(crop)=0.44, lambda(grass)=0.61, lambda(Intercept)=4.43
gamma(year)=-0.02, gamma(ppt)=-0.01, gamma(minTemp)=0.02, gamma(maxTemp)=-0.01, gamma(Intercept)=-0.08
                                            p(date)=-0.01, p(Intercept)=-0.63
Now since it's Poisson process model, I did exp^coefficient to compute these values, which gave me
                                           lambda(Intercept)=83.92, lambda(crop)=1.55,lambda(grass)=1.83
                                          gamma(Intercept)=0.92, gamma(year)=0.98,gamma(ppt)=0.99,gamma(minTemp)=1.02,gamma(maxTemp)=0.99
                                          p(Intercept)=0.53,p(date)=0.99

So does this mean, that if everything remains constant, the abundance will be 83.92, with per unit change in area under crop, abundance will increase by 1.55, with per unit change in area under grass abundance will increase by 1.83? Also is this the average values across sites? Or is this the value across study area?Similarly for gamma, which is population growth rate, so if everything remains constant gamma would be 0.92, with unit change in ppt it will change by 0.99, unit change in minTemp it will change by 1.02, unit change in maxTemp it will change by 0.99. Is this the right interpretation?

2) My second question is if there is another way of finding posterior distribution other than using ranef function. This function does not work on model as a result of doing averaging.

3) My third question is regarding predicting abundance against different covariates, for which I used modavgPred function

Actual code:
pred_data1<-data.frame(crop=seq(min(est_500$crop),max(est_500$crop),length.out = 108),
                      grass=seq(min(est_500$grass),max(est_500$grass),length.out = 108))
avg.pred<-modavgPred(list(m1.crop.grass.year.ppt.minTemp.date,m1.grass.year.minTemp.maxTemp.date),parm.type="lambda",newdata = pred_data1)
So avg.pred gives mean abundance across each route. 

But the plot of this predicted abundance against different covariates does not make sense at all. So am I doing something wrong?

If you can provide any suggestions on these questions, I would be really grateful.

Thanks tons!
Leo

messages.author: 4e956cc50ac3e075
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Model averaging in pcountOpen
parts:
Hi Leo,

Here are some suggestions:

1) You should not skim down the candidate model set when it comes to
compute model-averaged coefficients or predictions - you should be
using the entire set of models. You risk overestimating the effect of
certain parameters. Use all your models.

2) Instead of trying to average coefficients from each parameter, you
should be working on averaging predictions for some values of your
explanatory variables that are of interest to you. For example, if you
want to get predictions of abundance at different seasons, use each
model to make a prediction for lambda and then model-average those
predictions. If you want latent values (e.g., from ranef( )), you can
extract them from each model, and then model-average these values if
you want. You will have to use a couple of loops, but is not that
difficult to do.

3) If you want to present predictions in a plot, you need to vary only
one variable and keep the others constant. Otherwise, you will get
nonsensical lines or points. For example, if you want to show the
effect of crop on abundance, vary crop and keep all other variables
constant:


pred_data1<-data.frame(crop=seq(min(est_500$crop), 
max(est_500$crop),length.out = 30),
                       grass=mean(est_500$grass))

Then, you can model-average the predictions.

Good luck,

Marc

Hi Leo,

Here are some suggestions:

1) You should not skim down the candidate model set when it comes to
compute model-averaged coefficients or predictions - you should be
using the entire set of models. You risk overestimating the effect of
certain parameters. Use all your models.

2) Instead of trying to average coefficients from each parameter, you
should be working on averaging predictions for some values of your
explanatory variables that are of interest to you. For example, if you
want to get predictions of abundance at different seasons, use each
model to make a prediction for lambda and then model-average those
predictions. If you want latent values (e.g., from ranef( )), you can
extract them from each model, and then model-average these values if
you want. You will have to use a couple of loops, but is not that
difficult to do.

3) If you want to present predictions in a plot, you need to vary only
one variable and keep the others constant. Otherwise, you will get
nonsensical lines or points. For example, if you want to show the
effect of crop on abundance, vary crop and keep all other variables
constant:


pred_data1<-data.frame(crop=seq(min(est_500$crop), 
                       max(est_500$crop),length.out = 30),
                       grass=mean(est_500$grass))

Then, you can model-average the predictions.

Good luck,

Marc

parts:
Leo,


lambda is abundance during the first primary period, whereas gamma is recruitment between primary periods. Thus, if you have 5 primary periods, you will have 4 intervals (1 gamma for each). I suggest it is time for you to step back a little and dig deeper into what these models do and how to use them. There are a number of resources out there to get better acquainted with these methods (including the original papers).


Best of luck,


Marc
